legacy_report:
SOURCE: rStar2-Agent: Agentic Reasoning Technical Report. Ning Shang, Yifei Liu, Yi Zhu, Li Lyna Zhang et al. (Microsoft Research). arXiv:2508.20722v1, preprint, 28 Aug 2025.

COVERAGE: 22 of 22 pages read (87,268 chars). I read all body text, the tables, and the two appendix-style trace figures (Figs 10-11). I only skimmed the references, in the final ~20k chars. The extraction was clean apart from garbled equations. There are no results appendices.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Reward design: the paper uses a binary, answer-only outcome reward and rejects step-level rewards and tool-error penalties. Its reasons are tuning complexity and reward-hacking risk, which can also block early exploration.
  number: none (binary r in {0,1})
  setup: math RL, rule-based math-verify on the \boxed{} answer, integer-answer problems only.
  quote: "we do not adopt these approaches for two main reasons: (i) they introduce additional complexity, such as requiring careful human tuning and reward model construction; (ii) they are prone to reward hacking. For example, during early training, when the model's reasoning ability is still developing, step-level rewards or tool-error penalties can hinder effective exploration."
  where: p7 (Sec 2.2.3)
- claim: Under outcome-only reward, trajectories with failing tool calls still get reward 1 if the final answer is right. The tool-error rate in correct trajectories under naive GRPO plateaus instead of falling.
  number: ~15% (Qwen2.5-32B), ~10% (Qwen3-14B)
  setup: naive GRPO with Python tool, Fig 4.
  quote: "the ratio of tool-related errors in positively rewarded trajectories initially decreases but eventually stabilizes at a significant level, around 15% for Qwen2.5-32B and 10% for Qwen3-14B."
  where: p7
- claim: GRPO-RoC (Resample-on-Correct) fixes this without touching the reward. It oversamples 2G rollouts and keeps G. Negatives are downsampled uniformly (to keep failure diversity). Positives are sampled with probability inversely proportional to a penalty p_total = p_err + p_format.
  number: 2G=32 rollouts, keep G=16; p_err default 0.5 when there are no tool calls
  setup: Eq 4-6. p_err is the tool-error ratio. p_format penalises multiple <answer> tags, and a missing tag gets maximum downsample weight.
  quote: "Trajectories without tool calls are assigned a default perr = 0.5 to encourage tool usage" and "We then sample half of the positive rollouts with probability inversely proportional to ptotal"
  where: p8
- claim: Lesson on reward design: complex rule-based scoring biases the policy and penalises useful behaviour, so the paper keeps the reward minimal and handles quality through sampling. N-gram repetition detection hurt the response-length and reasoning scores. It mis-flagged legitimate repeated verification tool calls.
  number: none
  setup: tried as an extra RoC scoring term, following Phi-4-Reasoning's n-gram detection. No numbers given.
  quote: "Overly complex, rule-based rewards or scoring schemes can introduce bias, penalize useful behaviors, and fail to generalize across reasoning patterns."
  where: p13 (Sec 4.3.1)
- claim: DAPO-style overlong filtering did not help and raised the overlong ratio. Keeping truncated rollouts with negative reward was useful.
  number: none
  setup: the authors' own runs. Their hypothesis is that overlong responses are repetitive and need negative feedback.
  quote: "In our experiments, however, overlong filtering yields no benefits. On the contrary, it increases the ratios of overlong rollouts."
  where: p13
- claim: Main result. rStar2-Agent-14B reaches frontier-level math pass@1 in 510 RL steps on 64 MI300X GPUs in one week, from a non-reasoning SFT start.
  number: AIME24 80.6, AIME25 69.8, HMMT25 52.7, MATH-500 97.8
  setup: Qwen3-14B-Base, 16 samples per question, avg pass@1, 30K max tokens, temp 0.6, T=30 turns. Compared with o3-mini 79.6/77.0/53.0, DeepSeek-R1 79.8/70.0/44.4, Claude Opus 4.0 Think 76.0/69.2. Note that o3-mini beats it on AIME25 (77.0 vs 69.8) and HMMT25 (53.0 vs 52.7).
  quote: "achieving average pass@1 scores of 80.6% on AIME24 and 69.8% on AIME25, surpassing DeepSeek-R1 (671B) with significantly shorter responses."
  where: p1, Table 3 p14
- claim: Responses are shorter than comparable models.
  number: AIME24/AIME25 avg tokens: rStar2 9339.7/10943.4 vs R1-Zero 14246.8/17132.9, QwQ-32B 11868.4/15865.4, Qwen3-14B 14747.6/17521.9
  setup: Table 4, same eval setup.
  quote: "rStar2-Agent-14B 9339.7 10943.4"
  where: p15
- claim: RoC ablation. GRPO-RoC beats vanilla GRPO-with-Tool on AIME24 and AIME25 throughout training and gives shorter responses. GRPO with Tool in turn beats the no-tool DAPO baseline.
  number: no exact numbers in text (Fig 9 only)
  setup: 300 steps, G=16 for the baseline, other hyperparameters unchanged. DAPO scores are the reported ones after 2000 steps.
  quote: "Compared to GRPO with Tool, it consistently achieves higher reasoning accuracy on both AIME24 and AIME25 throughout training."
  where: p16 (Fig 9)
- claim: Agentic RL with tools beats CoT-only RL at fewer steps, on both base models.
  number: Qwen2.5-32B, 700 steps: 94.8 MATH-500 / 69.4 AIME24 / 57.3 AIME25 (rStar2) vs ReTool-32B 400 steps 93.4/67.0/49.3 (reasoning SFT) vs DAPO-32B >5000 steps 90.3/50.0/32.1. Qwen3-14B: DAPO-14B 2000 steps 45.2 AIME24 / 38.1 AIME25 vs rStar2 510 steps 80.6/69.8.
  setup: Table 6. On Qwen2.5-32B only stages 1-2 were run.
  quote: "rStar2-Agent achieves 2.4% and 8.0% higher accuracy on AIME24 and AIME25, respectively."
  where: p15-16
- claim: Infrastructure, code environment. A dedicated isolated service handles up to 45K tool calls per step at 0.3 s average latency. The design is a master node with a task queue, 32 send workers each batching up to 64 calls, and worker nodes with 1024 execution workers each. Answer verification is offloaded to the same service because the math verifier can be slow and blocks rollouts.
  number: 45K calls/step, 0.3 s, 32 send workers, batch 64, 1024 exec workers per node
  setup: runs on CPU cores of the 64-GPU cluster. Built on VERL v0.2 and SGLang. The text prints "high throughput (45 calls per step)", which looks like a typo for 45K.
  quote: "each training step can generate up to 45K tool calls. Even at this scale, the service achieves both high throughput (45 calls per step) and low latency (0.3 seconds per call, including scheduling and execution time)"
  where: p10
- claim: Infrastructure, scheduler. Static even allocation of rollouts causes GPU idle time (the longest rollout in each turn gates the rest). It also causes KV-cache overflow, where SGLang evicts half the in-progress rollouts and recomputes them. The fix is a scheduler that assigns rollouts by available KV-cache capacity, estimates K<N safely runnable rollouts per GPU, dispatches tool calls asynchronously, and refills as GPUs free up.
  number: none (no throughput speedup is reported)
  setup: Fig 7.
  quote: "When a GPU's KV cache exceed its capacity, SGLang evicts half of the in-progress rollouts, even if partial computation has already been completed."
  where: p10-11
- claim: Recipe. Non-reasoning SFT first, then three RL stages with short lengths. It uses 42K curated integer-answer problems, offline difficulty filtering for stage 3, and the optimizer reset plus reference update at stage 3.
  number: 8K to 12K to 12K tokens; batch 512 prompts; lr 1e-6; stage 1 ends at 300 steps; 510 steps total; stage-3 filtering leaves 17.3K problems (drops problems with 8/8 correct); T=10 turns in stages 1-2 and T=15 in stage 3
  setup: SFT data is 165K function-call examples, 30K instruction-following and 27K chat. SFT runs 3 epochs at lr 5e-6. Integer-only answers are required because verifiers fail on equivalent algebraic expressions. RL sources are 17K DAPO, 93K AoPS and 937 Project Euler problems, cleaned from over 100K to 42K using Qwen3-32B with 16 samples per problem.
  quote: "AIME24 improves from 3.3% (SFT) to 72.1% and AIME25 from 0% to 64.2%" (stage 1). Stage 2 reaches 77.0/64.8. Stage 3 reaches 80.6/69.8.
  where: p11-15
- claim: Algorithm changes to GRPO: KL penalty removed, Clip-Higher with eps_high 0.28, entropy loss removed. Sampling is at temperature 1.0 during training.
  number: eps_high 0.2 to 0.28
  setup: Sec 2.2.1.
  quote: "we remove the KL divergence penalty." and "increase εhigh from 0.2 to 0.28"
  where: p6
- claim: The post-SFT model is nearly useless at math but good at tools. SFT results: MATH-500 57.4, AIME24 3.33, AIME25 0, BFCL v3 63.1, IFEval 83.7, Arena-Hard 86.8.
  number: see list
  setup: Table 1.
  quote: "Our non-reasoning SFT 57.4 3.33 0 63.1 83.7 86.8"
  where: p11
- claim: Math-only RL transfers to science reasoning, not to tool use or alignment.
  number: GPQA-Diamond 42.1 (post-SFT) to 60.9 (vs DeepSeek-V3 59.1). BFCL v3 60.8 (SFT 63.1). IFEval 83.4 (SFT 83.7). Arena-Hard 86.6 (SFT 86.8).
  setup: Table 5, temp 0 for BFCL, IFEval and Arena-Hard.
  quote: "On non-reasoning tool-use and alignment tasks, the model shows no improvement but maintains performance comparable to our non-reasoning SFT baseline."
  where: p15. The intro claims it "excels at agentic tool use on BFCL v3" (p4), but the BFCL v3 score actually falls from 63.1 to 60.8, and it still beats DeepSeek-V3's 57.6.
- claim: Training collapse. After peak accuracy at step 510, continued RL collapsed both policy and reward. Several fixes failed.
  number: fixes tried were temperature 1.2, longer max response length, T from 10 to 20, higher clip-high, and an optimizer reset
  setup: 14B, stage 3. The authors say the failure mode has not been reported publicly and hypothesise a model-capacity ceiling.
  quote: "continued RL training leads to collapse in both policy and reward signals."
  where: p16-17
- claim: High-entropy tokens fall into two groups: forking tokens ("But before", "double-check") and new reflection tokens on tool responses. Tool-call code tokens themselves are low entropy.
  number: top 20% entropy tokens, 64 sampled trajectories
  setup: qualitative, Figs 10-11.
  quote: "coding tool call tokens themselves, which include Python code and code comments, are usually low-entropy."
  where: p19
- claim: Tool call interface. A JSON function-call format (name plus arguments) with <tool_call> and <tool_response> tags. The environment returns one of four outcomes: stdout, success without stdout, error with traceback, or timeout. Malformed JSON returns a parse error to the model. Max turns T bound the multi-turn rollout.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2.1.
  quote: "This structured approach provides a standardized, API-like interface that removes parsing ambiguity and clearly separates reasoning from execution."
  where: p5

LIMITS
- Math-only, with a Python interpreter as the only tool. The authors say whether this generalises to non-coding tools is open.
- Integer-answer problems only, because verifiers cannot reliably check algebraic equivalence.
- Stage 3 shows saturation and collapse at about 510 steps. The cause is only hypothesised.
- The Qwen2.5-32B comparison covers only stages 1-2. Cross-paper comparisons use different step counts and settings, so they are not controlled.
- The Fig 9 ablation is 300 steps, one setup, and the text gives no seeds or variance.
- No ablation isolates the RoC components (p_err vs p_format) or the infrastructure speedup. Scheduler gains are not quantified.
- The paper does not show the rollout oversampling cost (2G generation) against savings.
- Since the paper is from Aug 2025, later work may have superseded the benchmark standings.

BUILDS ON
GRPO (Shao et al. 2024, DeepSeekMath); DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al. 2025); DAPO (Yu et al. 2025: Clip-Higher, overlong filtering, 17K data); ReTool (Feng et al. 2025); ZTRL/Agent RL Scaling Law (Mai et al. 2025); ToRL (Li et al. 2025); ToolRL (Qian et al. 2025, tool-error penalties, which it contrasts with); Kimi-Researcher; VERL (Sheng et al. 2024, HybridFlow); SGLang (Zheng et al. 2024); forking-token and entropy work (Wang et al. 2025; Cui et al. 2025; Cheng et al. 2025); Phi-4-Reasoning (Abdin et al. 2025, n-gram repetition detection); OpenMathReasoning (Moshkov et al. 2025); ProRL (Liu et al. 2025a, optimizer reset); Yue et al. 2025b (RL cannot exceed the base model's capacity).

CODE: none. The text gives a few formulas (verbatim extractable): p_err = 0.5 if no tool calls, else num_error_tool_calls / num_all_tool_calls (Eq 4); p_format = 1 if no <answer> tags, else min(1, (num_answer_tags - 1)/num_turns) (Eq 5, garbled in extraction). Tool schema example: {"name": "execute_python_code_with_standard_io", "arguments": {"code": ..., "input": ...}} (Fig 3, p5). Code and recipes are at https://github.com/microsoft/rStar.

FIGURES (captions read from text, not rendered)
- Fig 2, p4: multi-turn rollout with the tool-call format. Shows how a trajectory interleaves reasoning, tool call and tool response.
- Fig 4, p7: tool error rate within correct trajectories, GRPO vs GRPO-RoC. Best single visual for the reward-design argument.
- Fig 5, p9: infrastructure and environment-service architecture (send workers, Redis queue, exec workers).
- Fig 6, p9: 45K concurrent tool calls with low latency.
- Fig 7, p10: static vs load-balanced KV-cache-aware scheduling.
- Fig 8, p14: AIME and response length across the three RL stages.
- Fig 9, p16: RoC ablation versus GRPO with Tool and DAPO.
- Figs 10-11, pp17-18: example traces with high-entropy tokens.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The equations are garbled in extraction. The scheduler design is described only qualitatively. One probable typo ("45 calls per step"). Stage 3 text says "final 385 steps of Stage 2", which is ambiguous against the 300-step stage 1 and 510 total. The Table 2 numbers for other methods are partly blank ("-"). I did not run the figures script, so the figure details above come from captions in the text only.
